title: The best Vector alternatives in 2026
summary: Vector gives you person-level identification and cross-web intent, then leaves the outreach to you. The best Vector alternatives in 2026, compared.
body_markdown:
The best Vector alternative is Artisan. Vector is a strong signal source: person-level identification plus contact-level intent across the web, month-to-month. But it is still a source you have to act on. Artisan identifies visitors, qualifies them, and has Ava, its AI BDR, run the outreach automatically. RB2B, Common Room, and Warmly suit narrower needs.

## Why do people look for a Vector alternative?


Because Vector is a great signal and not a system. It surfaces person-level identification and contact-level intent from across the web, which is more than most reveal tools see. Then it hands that intelligence to you. A rep still has to open the signal, decide the person fits, research the account, write something specific, and send it. Under real volume, most of that intelligence sits unworked while reps juggle everything else. For the basics, see[website visitor identification](https://www.artisan.co/blog/website-visitor-identification) .


The month-to-month pricing that makes Vector easy to start also makes it easy to outgrow. At $399-999 per month you get the signal, but as your needs widen you tend to bolt on a sequencer, a dialer, an enrichment source, and a reply workflow around it. Now you are running a stack again, stitching a best-of-breed signal to tools that were supposed to act on it.


There is also the honest ceiling on identification. Person-level reveal is a US phenomenon for every vendor, Vector included, because privacy rules keep the rest of the world at the company level. And even in the US, independent tests put realistic person-level match rates at 5-20% of traffic, so the signal is real but partial. None of this makes Vector bad. It makes it a component in a motion that still needs a worker.


## What is the best alternative to Vector?


Artisan, if you want the signal to end in a booked meeting rather than a task in someone's queue. Vector tells you who is showing intent. Artisan tells you who is showing intent, whether they fit your ICP, and shows you the personalized outreach that already went to them. Below, Artisan first, then six real alternatives, each with who it suits and who it does not.


### 1. Artisan: signals that become outreach


Artisan is an AI-first outbound platform built around Ava, an autonomous AI BDR. Intent signals and visitor identification are inputs to her, not the ceiling of the product. She identifies visitors at the person level on US traffic and at the company level globally on a 3.7B-IP identity graph with a published 92% accuracy rate, and she reads a wide signal set: funding rounds, new executive hires, tech-stack intent, Bombora-powered topic intent, champion job changes, and natural-language custom signals you define in plain English. Every identified, in-market contact runs through ICP qualification. For the how-to, see[how to identify anonymous website visitors](https://www.artisan.co/blog/how-to-identify-anonymous-website-visitors-and-turn-them-into-pipeline) .


The difference from Vector is what happens after the signal fires. Ava researches the account, writes a message specific to that person and that trigger, and sends it, on the autonomy setting you choose: review-and-approve, objections-only, or fully autonomous.[Ava Inbound](https://www.artisan.co/ai-sales-agent) adds a live chat agent that greets and qualifies visitors on your site and books meetings with CRM-owner routing, so intent that is ready to convert now gets handled immediately.


Chain of Events, the team behind RAISE Summit, sourced over $700k of ARR in six months with Ava, a 20x return on its investment. That is the value of pairing signal with activation: the intelligence turns into pipeline instead of a backlog of leads someone means to get to. For the how-to, see[identify anonymous website visitors](https://www.artisan.co/blog/identify-anonymous-website-visitors) .


**Best for:** teams from startup to enterprise that want intent and identification converted into outreach automatically, with governance and an audit trail. **Who should pick something else:** a team that wants only a best-of-breed intent feed to route into a stack it already runs. That is a narrower job, and a dedicated signal source fits it. **Pricing:** usage-based credits, no platform fee, free trial. See[artisan.co/pricing](https://www.artisan.co/pricing) .


### 2. RB2B: US person-level names to Slack


RB2B identifies US visitors at the person level and pushes names to Slack, from $79 to $199 per month per its plans. For a team that wants a name the moment someone hits the site, without Vector's broader intent layer or price, it is a focused, inexpensive pick. For the direct matchup, see[Artisan vs RB2B](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-rb2b) .


It stops at identification, and it is US-only at the person level. A Slack feed is a notification, not a qualification-and-outreach engine.


**Best for:** US teams that want low-cost person-level names and reps who act on them. **Who should pick something else:** teams that want intent beyond their own traffic, or the outreach automated. **Pricing:** $79-199/mo, per its plans.


### 3. Common Room: person-level buyer intelligence


Common Room aggregates person-level buyer signals from many sources into one intelligence layer, with entry around $2,500 per month. For a team that wants a broad signal picture and has ops to act on it, the aggregation is strong. Note the category event: Zoom announced it is acquiring Common Room in July 2026, so weigh the post-acquisition picture during evaluation.


It is intelligence, not activation. The outreach still runs wherever you route the signal.


**Best for:** teams wanting broad person-level signal aggregation with ops to act on it. **Who should pick something else:** teams that want the outreach built in, or that want to wait out the acquisition. **Pricing:** reported around $2,500/mo entry.


### 4. Warmly: live orchestration for small teams


Warmly pairs identification with real-time orchestration, showing who is on your site now and firing signal-based plays, with published tiers around $10-30K per year. For a small team that reacts in the moment, the live reveal and plays do real work.


Reps still run the follow-through. Warmly surfaces and orchestrates; a human writes and sends, so pipeline scales with headcount watching the feed. For the direct matchup, see[Artisan vs Warmly](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-warmly) .


**Best for:** small-to-mid teams that want live alerts and will staff the reaction. **Who should pick something else:** teams that want outreach automated rather than orchestrated for a person. **Pricing:** ~$10-30K/yr tiers, per its published pages.


### 5. Leadfeeder (Dealfront): EU company-level


Leadfeeder, now part of Dealfront, is the pick when your traffic is European. GDPR keeps EU identification at the company level, and Dealfront is built compliance-first for that reality, with strong European coverage and published tiers.


Company-level means you learn the account, not the person, and reveal only, with activation elsewhere. Post-merger product questions are worth asking during evaluation. For a related matchup, see[Leadfeeder vs Snitcher](https://www.artisan.co/blog/leadfeeder-vs-snitcher-which-should-you-choose-in-2026) .


**Best for:** EU-focused teams that need GDPR-first company identification. **Who should pick something else:** US teams wanting person-level names, or anyone wanting outreach automated. **Pricing:** published tiers on its site.


### 6. Factors: signals tied to analytics


Factors links company-level identification to account journey analytics and attribution, so you see how identified accounts move through the funnel. For a RevOps team that wants the reporting story alongside the leads, that is a real strength.


The ceiling is the category's: company-level identification and analytics, with activation left to whatever runs outreach.


**Best for:** RevOps teams that want visitor ID connected to analytics and attribution. **Who should pick something else:** teams wanting person-level identification or automated follow-up. **Pricing:** free 200 companies/mo; Lite $199/mo, Basic $6,000/yr, Growth $20,000/yr.


### 7. ZoomInfo WebSights: for existing ZoomInfo shops


If you run ZoomInfo, WebSights adds company-level identification inside it, with ZoomInfo's dataset for enrichment. Entry contracts for the broader platform are reported around $15K-plus per year. It is company-level, and a data platform first with execution added on. Buyers note ZoomInfo's contract terms have a reputation worth reading closely.


**Best for:** teams standardized on ZoomInfo that want visitor ID without a new vendor. **Who should pick something else:** teams wanting person-level US identification or built-in outreach. **Pricing:** add-on to ZoomInfo contracts.


## What is the best enterprise alternative to Vector?


Artisan. Vector's month-to-month signal model is easy to start and hard to govern at scale: there is no qualification layer deciding which of thousands of signals matter, no owner routing, no audit trail, and no outreach engine attached. Artisan runs the signal-to-outreach loop centrally. Sales ops can operate Ava for a large AE team who never log in, with plain-language escalation rules, do-not-contact enforcement across email, domain, social, and phone, and a full audit trail. Usage-based pricing keeps the cost flat as the team grows, rather than climbing with seats or with the number of point tools bolted around the signal. Artisan is SOC 2 Type II and GDPR compliant, with SSO, SAML, and role-based access.


## How we chose these alternatives


Four criteria, in order. First, how much of the job the tool does: signal alone, or signal through qualification to sent outreach. Second, data and signal depth: person-level versus company-level, own-traffic versus cross-web intent, US versus international coverage, and realistic match rates rather than headline figures. Third, pricing transparency: published tiers and month-to-month terms beat demo-gated quotes. Fourth, deployment fit: startup, enterprise, or only the middle. Artisan ranks first because it is the only entry that does the whole job, and it still notes that a team wanting a pure intent feed can buy a dedicated source. For the wider field, see[website visitor tracking tools](https://www.artisan.co/blog/website-visitor-tracking-tools) .


## Stay with Vector if


Keep Vector if what you value most is the signal itself: person-level identification plus contact-level intent across the web, on a month-to-month term you can leave whenever. If you have a mature stack and an ops team that reliably routes and acts on signals, Vector feeds it well, and the lack of annual lock-in is a real advantage while you test. The moment you find the intent piling up unworked, or you are bolting a sequencer, dialer, and reply workflow around it and calling that a system, that is your signal to consolidate into one that acts on its own signals.


For the wider category, see our guide to the[best website visitor identification tools](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-website-visitor-identification-tools) and how Ava works as an[AI BDR](https://www.artisan.co/blog/ai-bdr) .


## FAQ


**What does Vector do?** Vector combines person-level website visitor identification with contact-level intent data from across the web, so you see buying interest beyond your own traffic. It is priced month-to-month at $399-999. It is a signal source: it surfaces who is in-market and leaves the qualification and outreach to your team.


**What is the best alternative to Vector?** Artisan, for teams that want signals to end in booked meetings rather than a task queue. It identifies visitors, reads a wide signal set including intent, qualifies contacts against your ICP, and has Ava run personalized outreach automatically across email, social, and the dialer, with an inbound chat agent for buyers ready now.


**Can Vector identify international visitors at the person level?** No honest vendor can, and any that claims to is worth scrutinizing. Privacy rules keep non-US identification at the company level. Person-level reveal is a US phenomenon, and even there independent tests put realistic match rates at 5-20% of US traffic. Vector and Artisan both follow this constraint.


**Is Artisan more expensive than Vector?** They price differently. Vector charges a month-to-month subscription for signal. Artisan uses usage-based credits with no platform fee and no per-seat charge, covering identification, intent, and outreach in one line. If you would otherwise pair Vector with a sequencer, dialer, and reply tool, the consolidated cost usually favors Artisan. See[artisan.co/pricing](https://www.artisan.co/pricing) .


**What is the best enterprise alternative to Vector?** Artisan. It runs signal, qualification, and outreach centrally, so sales ops can operate it for a large AE team with owner routing, escalation rules, do-not-contact enforcement, and an audit trail. It is SOC 2 Type II and GDPR compliant, with SSO, SAML, and role-based access. A month-to-month signal feed does not scale to that governance.


**Do I still need outreach tools with Artisan?** No. Artisan is a full outbound platform, so identification, intent, ICP qualification, personalized multichannel outreach, reply handling, and meeting booking happen in one place. Ava, its[AI BDR](https://www.artisan.co/blog/ai-bdr) , owns that workflow end to end at the autonomy level you set, which is the difference from a standalone signal like Vector.


**What is the difference between Vector's intent data and Artisan's signals?** Vector delivers person-level and contact-level intent as a feed for you to act on. Artisan reads a wide signal set, including topic intent, funding, hiring, tech-stack, champion job changes, and custom natural-language triggers, and then acts on it automatically: Ava qualifies the contact and sends personalized outreach the moment a signal fires, rather than leaving it for a rep to work.
